# Ethical Marketing Campaign Design
## Market: **Japan** | Category: **Foods with Function Claims (機能性表示食品)** | Product: **Daily eye-comfort supplement (lutein + zeaxanthin + astaxanthin)**

> **Scope note:** Japan was selected because it has one of the world's most distinctive combinations of (a) strong cultural norms around modesty, safety and evidence, (b) a highly technical, notification-based health-claims regime, and (c) a market that has recently been shaken by a supplement safety scandal — making *ethics itself* a genuine competitive advantage. All regulatory references below reflect the Japanese framework and must be validated with local counsel and the Consumer Affairs Agency before execution; exact claim wording must match the notified text.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

| Element | Decision |
|---|---|
| **Market** | Japan (national, with Tokyo/Osaka/Nagoya metro weighting) |
| **Product** | "**MANAZASHI**" (眼差し — "the gaze"), a once-daily softgel: 10 mg lutein, 2 mg zeaxanthin, 4 mg astaxanthin |
| **Regulatory route** | Foods with Function Claims (FFC / 機能性表示食品), notified via systematic review to the Consumer Affairs Agency (CAA) |
| **Core target** | 45–64-year-old screen-intensive professionals and skilled-hand workers ("*me ga tsukareru* generation") |
| **Positioning** | *Quiet competence*: the least exaggerated, most transparent eye-comfort supplement in Japan |
| **Campaign idea** | **「よく見える、ふつうの日。」** — *"An ordinary day, seen clearly."* |
| **Ethical spine** | Four public pledges: Exact Claims · Easy Exit · Open Dossier · Doctor First |
| **Year-1 budget** | ¥600M (≈US$4M) working media + production |
| **Primary KPI** | 90-day continuation rate ≥ 55% with **zero** cancellation friction, complaint rate < 0.05%, JARO complaints = 0 |

---

## 2. Why This Market Requires a Purpose-Built Campaign

Japanese wellness consumers cannot be reached with globally templated supplement advertising. Four forces make transplanted creative fail — or become illegal.

**2.1 A cultural preference for understatement (控えめ)**
Hyperbole reads as untrustworthy. Superlatives, exclamation marks, "miracle," dramatic before/after visuals, and shouted urgency signal a low-quality operator. Persuasion works through *accumulated small proofs*: named researchers, factory footage, ingredient origin, third-party testing, a pharmacist's calm recommendation.

**2.2 *Anshin* (安心 — peace of mind) as the dominant purchase driver**
Japanese consumers buy safety before efficacy. Country of manufacture, GMP certification, allergen transparency, batch traceability, and a visible responsible person outrank claimed benefit strength. The March 2024 red-yeast-rice (紅麹) health-damage incident collapsed sector trust and triggered tighter FFC rules (mandatory adverse-event reporting, GMP requirements for supplement-form FFC products). **Transparency is now the highest-ROI marketing asset in this category.**

**2.3 *Kenkō jumyō* (健康寿命 — healthy life expectancy) as national narrative**
Government policy ("Health Japan 21", third term) frames health as *maintaining independent function*, not youthfulness. The culturally resonant motivation is **not** "look younger" but "**keep doing the work and the roles I care about, and not become a burden (迷惑) to others.**" This must be activated *positively* — as continuity and contribution — never as guilt or fear of dependency.

**2.4 Relational and seasonal purchase logic**
- A large share of senior-targeted supplement purchases are made *by adult children for parents*, and via gifting seasons (お中元 / お歳暮) and New Year resolution moments.
- Trial behavior is driven by **お試し (o-tameshi) samples**, drugstore pharmacist advice, and point economies (Rakuten, PayPay, V-Point) rather than discount shouting.
- Media consumption is generationally stratified: LINE and Yahoo! Japan skew 50+, YouTube is universal, Instagram indexes to women 30–45, TV/radio/newspaper inserts still convert 60+.

---

## 3. Regulatory & Advertising-Norms Map (Compliance Foundation)

| Instrument | What it constrains | Campaign implication |
|---|---|---|
| **Pharmaceuticals & Medical Devices Act (薬機法), Art. 68** + the "Scope of Unapproved Drugs" notification | A food becomes an illegal unapproved *drug* if advertising claims disease treatment/prevention, effects on body structure/function beyond permitted claims, or drug-like dosing | Ban all mention of cataracts, glaucoma, macular degeneration, "vision recovery," "cures," "prevents." No "服用" (dosing) language — use 「1日1粒を目安にお召し上がりください」 |
| **Health Promotion Act (健康増進法), Art. 65** | False or exaggerated health claims for food | No implication of guaranteed results; no "everyone experiences…" |
| **Act against Unjustifiable Premiums & Misleading Representations (景品表示法)** | Misleading quality/price claims; CAA may demand substantiation within ~15 days; surcharge penalties; **stealth-marketing rule in force since 1 Oct 2023** | Every claim needs a pre-built evidence dossier. **All** paid influencer/affiliate content must be clearly labeled 「広告」/「PR」 in-frame, not buried in hashtags. No unsubstantiated "No.1 / 売上No.1" claims |
| **FFC system (機能性表示食品)** | Notification (not approval) 60+ days pre-launch; claim wording fixed; mandatory disclaimers; target = healthy adults only | Advertising **must not deviate** from notified wording; must not target patients, children, or pregnant women; must carry the "not individually evaluated by the CAA" statement and the balanced-diet statement |
| **Act on Specified Commercial Transactions (特商法, 2022 amendments)** | Final-confirmation-screen disclosure for subscriptions; prohibition of misleading auto-renewal | Subscription terms, total cost, and one-click cancellation must be shown on the same screen as the order button |
| **APPI (personal data, 2022 amendments)** | Consent, cross-border transfer, cookie/ID handling | No health-inference targeting; opt-in only; JP-resident data hosting |
| **Self-regulation:** JARO, JHNFA guidelines, Tokyo Metropolitan Government health-food ad monitoring, platform policies (Yahoo!/Google/LINE ad review) | Tone, testimonials, imagery | No before/after imagery, no white-coat actors, no doctor endorsement of the product, testimonials must be real, verifiable, individually consented, and captioned as individual experience |

**Compliance gate:** No asset ships without sign-off from (1) internal regulatory affairs, (2) external Japanese *yakuji* advertising counsel, (3) the medical advisory board.

---

## 4. Ethical Framework — The Four Public Pledges

Rather than treating ethics as a legal minimum, we make it the **campaign message**. Each pledge is published in plain Japanese on-pack, on-site, and in all long-form assets.

**① 正確に言います — "We say exactly what the research says."**
We publish the notified claim verbatim, the systematic review, the effect size, the study population, and — explicitly — **what the product does not do**. Copy includes a stated limitation, e.g. 「視力そのものが良くなるわけではありません。」("This does not improve eyesight itself.")

**② いつでもやめられます — "You can stop any time."**
No lock-in, no minimum terms, no retention dark patterns. Cancellation is available online in one screen and by phone with no upsell script. This is *advertised*, not hidden — a direct rebuke of the category's worst practice and a strong trust signal in Japan's mail-order market.

**③ 全部見せます — "The whole dossier is open."**
QR code on pack → batch-level certificates of analysis, heavy-metal and residual-pesticide results, GMP certificate, ingredient origin map, allergen data, and an adverse-event reporting form with a 72-hour response commitment.

**④ お医者さんが先です — "The doctor comes first."**
Every asset that mentions eye discomfort directs consumers to an ophthalmologist for symptoms (pain, sudden change, floaters, distorted vision) and states that the product is not a substitute for examination or medication. In-store materials include an eye-clinic finder.

### What we will *not* do (binding internal red lines)
1. No fear appeals about blindness, dementia, or dependency.
2. No implication that supplements can replace medical care or eye exams.
3. No targeting of under-20s, pregnant/nursing women, or diagnosed patients; no lookalike audiences built on health inferences.
4. No "personal experience" testimonials implying disease outcomes; no paid reviews; no undisclosed affiliates.
5. No auto-enrollment, negative-option billing, hidden minimum terms, or countdown-timer scarcity.
6. No outbound cold-calling of consumers aged 70+, and no in-home sales.
7. No ageist or ableist framing ("don't be a burden," "old eyes"); no body-shaming.
8. No unverified sustainability or "natural = safe" claims (greenwashing is itself actionable under 景品表示法).
9. No creative that requires reading text smaller than the access

# Critique: "Ethical Marketing Campaign Design — Japan / MANAZASHI"

## Summary judgment
The strategic foundation is unusually strong for this brief — the market rationale, the *anshin* / 健康寿命 / 控えめ analysis, and the regulatory map are specific, current, and mostly accurate. But the deliverable **is not a campaign**. It stops mid-sentence in Section 4, and everything the brief actually asks for downstream (creative executions, channel/media plan, sampling and retail mechanics, budget allocation, timeline, measurement, risk/crisis response) is missing. Several load-bearing elements also contradict each other or the law they cite.

---

## 1. Blocking issues

**1.1 The output is truncated.** It ends: *"No creative that requires reading text smaller than the access"*. Red line #9 is incomplete, and Sections 5+ do not exist. The Executive Summary promises a campaign idea, a ¥600M budget, metro weighting, and KPIs — none of these are developed anywhere. # Ethical Marketing Campaign Design
## Market: **Japan** | Category: **Foods with Function Claims (機能性表示食品)** | Product: **Daily eye-comfort supplement (lutein + zeaxanthin + astaxanthin)**

> **Scope note:** Japan was selected because it has one of the world's most distinctive combinations of (a) strong cultural norms around modesty, safety and evidence, (b) a highly technical, notification-based health-claims regime, and (c) a market that has recently been shaken by a supplement safety scandal — making *ethics itself* a genuine competitive advantage. All regulatory references below reflect the Japanese framework and must be validated with local counsel and the Consumer Affairs Agency before execution; exact claim wording must match the notified text.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

| Element | Decision |
|---|---|
| **Market** | Japan (national, with Tokyo/Osaka/Nagoya metro weighting) |
| **Product** | "**MANAZASHI**" (眼差し — "the gaze"), a once-daily softgel: 10 mg lutein, 2 mg zeaxanthin, 4 mg astaxanthin |
| **Regulatory route** | Foods with Function Claims (FFC / 機能性表示食品), notified via systematic review to the Consumer Affairs Agency (CAA) |
| **Core target** | 45–64-year-old screen-intensive professionals and skilled-hand workers ("*me ga tsukareru* generation") |
| **Positioning** | *Quiet competence*: the least exaggerated, most transparent eye-comfort supplement in Japan |
| **Campaign idea** | **「よく見える、ふつうの日。」** — *"An ordinary day, seen clearly."* |
| **Ethical spine** | Four public pledges: Exact Claims · Easy Exit · Open Dossier · Doctor First |
| **Year-1 budget** | ¥600M (≈US$4M) working media + production |
| **Primary KPI** | 90-day continuation rate ≥ 55% with **zero** cancellation friction, complaint rate < 0.05%, JARO complaints = 0 |

---

## 2. Why This Market Requires a Purpose-Built Campaign

Japanese wellness consumers cannot be reached with globally templated supplement advertising. Four forces make transplanted creative fail — or become illegal.

**2.1 A cultural preference for understatement (控えめ)**
Hyperbole reads as untrustworthy. Superlatives, exclamation marks, "miracle," dramatic before/after visuals, and shouted urgency signal a low-quality operator. Persuasion works through *accumulated small proofs*: named researchers, factory footage, ingredient origin, third-party testing, a pharmacist's calm recommendation.

**2.2 *Anshin* (安心 — peace of mind) as the dominant purchase driver**
Japanese consumers buy safety before efficacy. Country of manufacture, GMP certification, allergen transparency, batch traceability, and a visible responsible person outrank claimed benefit strength. The March 2024 red-yeast-rice (紅麹) health-damage incident collapsed sector trust and triggered tighter FFC rules (mandatory adverse-event reporting, GMP requirements for supplement-form FFC products). **Transparency is now the highest-ROI marketing asset in this category.**

**2.3 *Kenkō jumyō* (健康寿命 — healthy life expectancy) as national narrative**
Government policy ("Health Japan 21", third term) frames health as *maintaining independent function*, not youthfulness. The culturally resonant motivation is **not** "look younger" but "**keep doing the work and the roles I care about, and not become a burden (迷惑) to others.**" This must be activated *positively* — as continuity and contribution — never as guilt or fear of dependency.

**2.4 Relational and seasonal purchase logic**
- A large share of senior-targeted supplement purchases are made *by adult children for parents*, and via gifting seasons (お中元 / お歳暮) and New Year resolution moments.
- Trial behavior is driven by **お試し (o-tameshi) samples**, drugstore pharmacist advice, and point economies (Rakuten, PayPay, V-Point) rather than discount shouting.
- Media consumption is generationally stratified: LINE and Yahoo! Japan skew 50+, YouTube is universal, Instagram indexes to women 30–45, TV/radio/newspaper inserts still convert 60+.

---

## 3. Regulatory & Advertising-Norms Map (Compliance Foundation)

| Instrument | What it constrains | Campaign implication |
|---|---|---|
| **Pharmaceuticals & Medical Devices Act (薬機法), Art. 68** + the "Scope of Unapproved Drugs" notification | A food becomes an illegal unapproved *drug* if advertising claims disease treatment/prevention, effects on body structure/function beyond permitted claims, or drug-like dosing | Ban all mention of cataracts, glaucoma, macular degeneration, "vision recovery," "cures," "prevents." No "服用" (dosing) language — use 「1日1粒を目安にお召し上がりください」 |
| **Health Promotion Act (健康増進法), Art. 65** | False or exaggerated health claims for food | No implication of guaranteed results; no "everyone experiences…" |
| **Act against Unjustifiable Premiums & Misleading Representations (景品表示法)** | Misleading quality/price claims; CAA may demand substantiation within ~15 days; surcharge penalties; **stealth-marketing rule in force since 1 Oct 2023** | Every claim needs a pre-built evidence dossier. **All** paid influencer/affiliate content must be clearly labeled 「広告」/「PR」 in-frame, not buried in hashtags. No unsubstantiated "No.1 / 売上No.1" claims |
| **FFC system (機能性表示食品)** | Notification (not approval) 60+ days pre-launch; claim wording fixed; mandatory disclaimers; target = healthy adults only | Advertising **must not deviate** from notified wording; must not target patients, children, or pregnant women; must carry the "not individually evaluated by the CAA" statement and the balanced-diet statement |
| **Act on Specified Commercial Transactions (特商法, 2022 amendments)** | Final-confirmation-screen disclosure for subscriptions; prohibition of misleading auto-renewal | Subscription terms, total cost, and one-click cancellation must be shown on the same screen as the order button |
| **APPI (personal data, 2022 amendments)** | Consent, cross-border transfer, cookie/ID handling | No health-inference targeting; opt-in only; JP-resident data hosting |
| **Self-regulation:** JARO, JHNFA guidelines, Tokyo Metropolitan Government health-food ad monitoring, platform policies (Yahoo!/Google/LINE ad review) | Tone, testimonials, imagery | No before/after imagery, no white-coat actors, no doctor endorsement of the product, testimonials must be real, verifiable, individually consented, and captioned as individual experience |

Rather than treating ethics as a legal minimum, we make it the **campaign message**. Each pledge is published in plain Japanese on-pack, on-site, and in all long-form assets.

**① 正確に言います — "We say exactly what the research says."**
We publish the notified claim verbatim, the systematic review, the effect size, the study population, and — explicitly — **what the product does not do**. Copy includes a stated limitation, e.g. 「視力そのものが良くなるわけではありません。」("This does not improve eyesight itself.")

**② いつでもやめられます — "You can stop any time."**
No lock-in, no minimum terms, no retention dark patterns. Cancellation is available online in one screen and by phone with no upsell script. This is *advertised*, not hidden — a direct rebuke of the category's worst practice and a strong trust signal in Japan's mail-order market.

**③ 全部見せます — "The whole dossier is open."**
QR code on pack → batch-level certificates of analysis, heavy-metal and residual-pesticide results, GMP certificate, ingredient origin map, allergen data, and an adverse-event reporting form with a 72-hour response commitment.

**④ お医者さんが先です — "The doctor comes first."**
Every asset that mentions eye discomfort directs consumers to an ophthalmologist for symptoms (pain, sudden change, floaters, distorted vision) and states that the product is not a substitute for examination or medication. In-store materials include an eye-clinic finder.

8. No unverified sustainability or "natural = safe" claims (greenwashing is itself actionable under 景品表示法).

## 2. Why templated supplement advertising fails here

Japanese wellness communication is not a translation problem. Four forces make imported creative ineffective — or unlawful.

**2.1 Understatement (控えめ) is a credibility technology.** Hyperbole reads as a warning sign. Superlatives, exclamation marks, "miracle", dramatic before/after visuals and countdown urgency are the signature of low-quality operators, and several are independently prohibited by platform ad policy. Persuasion here is *cumulative*: a named researcher, a factory floor, an ingredient-origin map, a batch certificate, a pharmacist who does not oversell. Our creative task is not to find one big idea; it is to stack twelve small verifiable ones. **[EVIDENCE — supported by JARO complaint patterns and platform ad policies; to be reinforced with our own copy-test data]**

**2.2 *Anshin* (安心) outranks efficacy.** Manufacturing country, GMP status, allergen and batch transparency, and a visible accountable human tend to weigh more heavily than benefit magnitude. The 紅麹 incident collapsed sector trust and produced tighter FFC obligations, including mandatory reporting of physician-confirmed health damage and GMP requirements for supplement-form FFC. **The practical consequence for us: transparency is the highest-return media asset in the category.** **[HYPOTHESIS on relative weighting — to be quantified via MaxDiff in the §14 quant wave; LAW on the regulatory changes]**

**2.3 *Kenkō jumyō* (健康寿命) is the national frame.** Public health policy frames health as maintained *function and independence*, not youth. The resonant motivation is therefore not "look younger" but "keep doing the work and the roles I care about." Critically, the adjacent emotion — fear of becoming a burden (迷惑) — is culturally live and **we refuse to use it**. Continuity and contribution are motivating; dependency-shaming is exploitative and is a hard red line (§7.2). **[EVIDENCE for policy framing; POLICY for the refusal]**

**2.4 Purchase logic is relational, seasonal and pharmacist-mediated.** Three mechanics matter more than advertising weight: the **¥300–500 お試し (o-tameshi) trial**; **drugstore pharmacist/registered-seller recommendation**; and **gifting/新年 resolution moments**, including purchases made by adult children for parents. Media consumption is generationally stratified (LINE and Yahoo! Japan skew 50+; YouTube is near-universal; terrestrial/BS TV, radio and newspaper inserts still convert 65+). §9 and §10 are built directly on this stratification rather than merely noting it. **[HYPOTHESIS on gifting/child-purchase share — sized in research wave 1 before trade budget is committed]**
